# FSI Publications Style Sheet - Border Security & Public Safety series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Vance Tolliver, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style except where noted. Headlines in title case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "illegal alien" (statutory term, 8 U.S.C. 1365) in body copy; "noncitizen" when quoting federal data that uses it.
A3. Lead with public safety and victims. The series argues for stronger interior enforcement; copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and date. Population, timeframe and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Prefer federal primary sources (ICE, USSC, GAO, BJS) over secondary analyses.
B3. Counter-research (e.g. Cato's Texas DPS analyses): appendix only, one line, followed by CIS's methodological critique.
B4. Charts: FSI navy #1F3A5F / red #B22234; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.
C2. Fact sheet: every stat footnoted.

messages.content:
# Outline - Brief No. 14 (B. Kessler, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: federal data show a serious public-safety cost from illegal immigration and weak interior enforcement; Congress should (1) fund detention of criminal aliens on the non-detained docket, (2) mandate ICE detainer compliance / penalise sanctuary jurisdictions, (3) expand 287(g), (4) require DHS public reporting on releases.
Sections: 1. The non-detained docket. 2. Federal sentencing. 3. State data (Texas). 4. Sanctuary policies and detainers. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Victim stories: Laken Riley (Athens, GA, Feb 2024) is fine to mention briefly; do not invent others.

# Source tables - Brief No. 14 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. ICE non-detained docket - homicide convictions
- 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions on ICE's non-detained docket as of 21 July 2024.
- Source: ICE letter (Patrick J. Lechleitner) to Rep. Tony Gonzales, 25 Sep 2024.
- Context (DHS/ICE statements, Sep-Oct 2024): records go back roughly four decades and cover entries under all administrations; the non-detained docket includes people currently incarcerated by federal, state or local authorities; ICE did not say how many.

## T2. Federal sentencing, FY2024 (U.S. Sentencing Commission, Quick Facts: Non-U.S. Citizen Federal Offenders, FY2024)
- Non-U.S. citizens: 21,304 individuals = 34.7% of all individuals sentenced.
- Primary guideline for noncitizens: immigration 72.3%; drug trafficking 17.6%; other 10.1%.
- 88.7% of noncitizens sentenced were illegal aliens; 8.5% legal aliens.
- GAO-24-107598: number of noncitizens sentenced fell 27% FY2018 -> FY2023.

## T3. Texas DPS conviction data
- Cato Institute (A. Nowrasteh), Texas DPS data 2013-2022: homicide conviction rate per 100,000 - illegal immigrants 2.2, native-born Americans 3.0 (illegal immigrants 26% less likely to be convicted of homicide). Cato also finds lower all-crime arrest/conviction rates; notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses.
- Center for Immigration Studies: disputes Cato's denominators (argues Cato misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration) and concludes illegal immigrants have higher conviction rates in Texas.

Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens | United States Sentencing Commission 

 Skip to main content

 Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens

 Of the 66,662 cases reported to the Commission in fiscal year 2025, 28,886 involved non-U.S. citizens. 1 Non-U.S. citizens accounted for 44% of all individuals sentenced in fiscal year 2025.
 Click the cover for the PDF handout or learn more below.  
 Individual and Offense Characteristics

 94% of non-U.S. citizens sentenced in the federal system were men.

 95% were Hispanic, 2% were Black, 2% were White, and 2% were Other races.

 Their average age was 37 years. 

 92% were illegal aliens, 6% were legal aliens, 1% were extradited aliens, and 1% were unknown status.

 66% were from Mexico, 10% from Honduras, 8% from Guatemala, 3% from El Salvador, 3% from the Dominican Republic, and 11% originated from other countries.

 The most common guidelines under which non-U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Immigration (79%); Drug Trafficking (12%); Fraud (3%);  Firearms (2%); Money Laundering (1%); and Administration of Justice (1%). 2 

 59% had little or no prior criminal history (Criminal History Category I); 21% were CHC II;
 13% were CHC III;
 4% were CHC IV;
 2% were CHC V;
 1% were CHC VI.

 The top five districts for sentenced non-U.S. citizens were: Western District of Texas (7,346);
 Southern District of Texas (4,814);
 District of Arizona (2,576);
 District of New Mexico (2,150);
 Southern District of California (747).

 The top five districts where sentenced non-U.S. citizens comprised the highest proportion of the overall caseloads were: District of Northern Mariana Islands (82%);
 Western District of Texas (80%);
 District of New Mexico (80%);
 Southern District of Texas (72%);
 District of Arizona (66%).

 Punishment
 The average sentence for non-U.S. citizens was 21 months. 3 

 97% were sentenced to prison.

 9% were convicted of an offense carrying a mandatory minimum penalty.

 Sentences Relative to the Guideline Range
 79% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were under the Guidelines Manual. 63% were within the guideline range.

 10% were Early Disposition Program (EDP) departures. 4 The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 3% were substantial assistance departures. The average sentence reduction was 44%. 

 2% were some other downward departure. The average sentence reduction was 42%. 

 Less than 1% were upward departures. The average sentence increase was 106%. 

 21% of sentences for non-U.S. citizens were variances. 15% were downward variances. The average sentence reduction was 39%. 

 6% were upward variances. The average sentence increase was 65%. 

 The average guideline minimum and the average sentence imposed have fluctuated over the past five years. The average guideline minimum was 33 months in fiscal year 2021 and 25 months in fiscal year 2025.

 The average sentence imposed was 25 months in fiscal year 2021 and 21 months in fiscal year 2025.

 1 Cases with incomplete sentencing information were excluded from the analysis.
 2  The most common guidelines under which U.S. citizens were sentenced include: Drug Trafficking (36%); Firearms (21%); Fraud (12%); Immigration (7%); Child Pornography (4%); Sexual Abuse (4%);  and Robbery (3%).
 3  The average sentence for U.S. citizens was 71 months.
 4  “Early Disposition Program" (or EDP) departures are departures where the government sought a sentence below the guideline range because the defendant participated in the government’s Early Disposition Program, through which cases are resolved in an expedited manner. See USSG §5K3.1.
 SOURCE: United States Sentencing Commission, FY 2021 through FY 2025 Datafiles, USSCFY21-USSCFY25.

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics 

 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations Statistics

 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement's Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) officers enforce immigration laws within the interior to preserve national security and public safety.

 ERO manages all aspects of the immigration enforcement process, including the identification, arrest, detention and removal of aliens who are subject to removal or are unlawfully present in the United States.

 Like all law enforcement agencies, ERO officers prioritize their enforcement actions based on agency and department priorities, funding and capacity. ERO operations are flexible enough to allow its officers to respond to events such as spikes in border crossings, modifications to U.S. laws, pandemics, and natural disasters at home and abroad.

 The following dashboards present for the first time information and trends in arrests, detentions, removals and alternatives to detention as of December 31, 2024.

We will continue to evaluate and enhance how the agency communicates measurable data to best inform how our officers and special agents perform their law enforcement missions in accordance with departmental and agency priorities.” — ICE Deputy Director and Senior Official Performing the Duties of the Director Patrick J. Lechleitner

 Arrest Statistics
 ERO enforces laws by arresting immigration violators in the interior of the United States. It relies on statutory law enforcement authority to identify and arrest aliens who may present threats to national security or public safety, or who otherwise undermine the integrity of U.S. immigration laws. ERO uses targeted, intelligence-driven operations to prioritize its enforcement actions in ways that help protect communities nationwide. While ERO primarily conducts administrative arrests of aliens it has probable cause to believe are removable from the United States, it also has the authority to execute criminal arrest warrants and initiate prosecutions for criminal activity, including immigration-related crimes. ERO officers assigned to task forces also help target and apprehend foreign fugitives in the United States who are wanted for crimes here and abroad by working with domestic and international partners.
 Arrests by country of citizenship and criminal history: ERO arrests are broken down by country of citizenship and categories of criminal history that include people with: U.S. criminal convictions.

*This category includes those who have repeatedly violated U.S. law by reentering after deportation, immigration fugitives with an executable final order of removal, and international fugitives wanted for crimes committed abroad.
 For fiscal years 2021 and 2022, this category also includes individuals apprehended while attempting to unlawfully enter the United States after January 1, 2021.

 ERO arrests over time: Historically, ERO most commonly arrests immigration violators with convictions involving DUI, drug possession, assault and criminal (non-civil) traffic offenses such as hit-and-run or leaving the scene of an accident.
 Arrests by Area of Responsibility (AOR): ERO has 24 field offices, which are geographic areas of responsibility , around the country, each headed by a field office director.

 Maintenance Alert

 Detention Statistics
 ERO oversees the civil immigration detention of one of the most diverse and rapidly changing detained populations in the world. The ERO Headquarters Custody Management and ICE Health Service Corps divisions help officers in the field manage the detained population and ensure detained aliens’ health and safety, ensure compliance with ICE’s detention standards, and provide medical care — including mental health care — to detained individuals.
 ICE detains individuals as necessary, including to secure their presence for immigration proceedings and removal from the United States. ICE also detains those who are subject to mandatory detention under U.S. immigration law and those a supervisor has determined are public safety or flight risks.
 After ICE arrests and processes individuals for administrative immigration violations or CBP and other state, local and federal law enforcement partners turn them over to ICE, officials may detain them while their immigration cases are pending or release them under a form of supervision. Both ICE and the Department of Justice’s Executive Office for Immigration Review — the office that oversees the immigration court system — can impact custody status at various points during a alien's immigration proceedings.
 Officials make custody determinations on an individual basis, taking into account all facets of a person’s situation, including their immigration history and criminal records. Authorities also consider family ties, humanitarian issues and whether a person may be a flight risk.
 Whenever possible, ICE seeks to house detained individuals within the geographical areas of their arrests to minimize their time in ICE custody and keep them close to family, friends and legal representatives.
 Most detained individuals are transfers from CBP following arrests at the border. ICE is legally obligated to detain some of these people, including those with certain criminal histories.
 If an alien or their representative believes they should not be subject to enforcement, detention or removal, they should contact their local ERO field office to request a case review or initiate the ICE Case Review process. People who want to contact ICE about their cases should first notify their local ERO field office via email with supporting documentation for an initial review.

 Individuals with pending criminal charges.
 Those with no convictions or pending charges but who have broken U.S. immigration laws.*

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act 

 Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act

 ICE’s 287(g) Program
 The Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996 added Section 287(g) to the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), authorizing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to delegate state and local law enforcement officers the authority to perform specified immigration officer functions under ICE’s direction and oversight.
 The Program enhances the safety and security of our nation’s communities by allowing ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) to partner with state, local, and tribal law enforcement agencies to identify and remove criminal aliens who are amenable to removal from the United States.
 ICE recognizes the importance of its relationships with law enforcement partners—including state and local agencies—to carry out its critical mission.
 Through the delegation of specified immigration officer duties, the program allows ICE to enhance collaboration with state and local law enforcement partners to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.
 What’s in It for Your Law Enforcement Agency?
 The 287(g) Program benefits state and local law enforcement agencies in several ways — but most notably, it helps you keep your community safe from potentially dangerous criminal aliens. Your law enforcement officers will get access to ICE resources and training. ICE covers the cost of training (see the later section, “287(g) Training Available to State and Local Law Enforcement,” for more information).
 Your agency or office may be eligible for the Department of Justice’s State Criminal Alien Assistance Program . This Department of Justice program administers SCAAP awards and provides federal funding to states and political subdivisions of states, including municipalities that incur costs for incarcerating certain criminal aliens. This is entirely separate from the 287(g) program. 
 ICE 287(g) Program Map

 287(g) Program Models
 ICE Enforcement and Removal Operations operates three 287(g) models:
 The  Jail Enforcement Model allows designated immigration officers to identify and process removable aliens who have pending or active criminal charges.
 The  Task Force Model  enhances public safety and national security by allowing designated immigration officers to enforce limited immigration authority while performing routine police duties or as an active participant in an ICE-led task force.
 The Warrant Service Officer Model allows designated immigration officers to serve and execute administrative warrants on aliens in their custody.
 How Can Your Agency Participate in the ICE 287(g) Program?
 On January 20, 2025, President Donald J. Trump issued Executive Order (EO) 14159, Protecting the American People Against Invasion . This EO requires ICE to authorize State and local law enforcement officials, as the Secretary of Homeland Security determines are qualified and appropriate, under section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act to the maximum extent permitted by law. Several states, including but not limited to Georgia and Florida, have passed, or are considering, State legislation mandating law enforcement agencies (LEAs) seek out or enter into memorandums of agreement (MOA) with ICE pursuant to a partnership under the 287(g) Program.
 Participation in the 287(g) Program is limited to LEAs only. LEAs interested in participating in the 287(g) Program must sign an MOA with ICE. LEAs will nominate officers to participate in the 287(g) Program. Nominees must possess U.S. citizenship, complete and pass a background investigation, and have knowledge of and have enforced laws and regulations related to law enforcement activities at their jurisdictions. Task Force Model nominees must also have at least two (2) years of total law enforcement officer experience. Nominees will receive training at the expense of ICE related to the immigration duties pertinent to the applicable MOA.
 LEAs interested in becoming a law enforcement partner under the 287(g) Program must submit a signed MOA to ICE at ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . These forms can be found below.

 Please click on the applicable MOA (fillable), complete and sign in its entirety, and email back to the 287(g) program team at: ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov . 

 JEM MOA (fillable) 

 TFM MOA (fillable) 

 WSO MOA (fillable) 

 How Can I Convince My Chief or Sheriff to Participate in 287(g)?
 ICE has several resources, including this page, that can help you show your chief, sheriff or team all the benefits the 287(g) Program provides. From here, you can also download and print ICE’s:
 287(g) fact sheet. 
 287(g) brochure. 
 If you have any questions about participating in the ICE 287(g) program, how to complete the necessary forms, what is required, or would like additional information, please do not hesitate to email ERO287g@ice.dhs.gov ; your inquiry will be promptly answered within one business day.
 287(g) Participating Agencies
 As of October 15, 2026 10:58 am ICE has signed 2,679 Memorandums of Agreement for ​287(g) programs covering ​38 states and 2 ​U.S. Territories. ​These include JEM agreements ​with 183 ​law ​enforcement ​agencies ​in ​29 ​states and 1 ​U.S. Territory, 287(g) ​WSO agreements ​with ​572 ​law ​enforcement ​agencies ​in ​34 ​states, and 287(g) TFM ​agreements ​with 1,924 agencies ​in ​32 ​states and 2 ​U.S. Territories.

 Background

 The Immigration and Nationality Act (INA, Title 8 of the U .S. Code ) authorizes and sometimes requires the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to detain aliens ( foreign nationals ) who are subject to removal from the United States. This authority allows DHS to detain aliens who pose a threat to public safety, ensures that such individuals appear at immigration removal hearings, and permits DHS to remove an individual more effectively after an order of removal has been issued. Detained aliens represent what is known as the detained docket . However, DHS has broad discretion to release from custody those aliens who are not subject to mandatory detention or do not pose a threat or flight risk. These individuals represent the non-detained docket (NDD) .

 Supervision of aliens on the detained and the non-detained docke ts is the responsibility of Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) within DHS's Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) . ERO may arrest any alien who is believed to have violated U.S. immigration laws and remove any alien who has received a final removal order . The INA generally requires detention for applicants for admission who are removable, aliens removable on specified criminal and terrorist-related grounds, and those with final removal orders.

 The INA also grants DHS discretion to either detain or release from custody all other aliens in pending removal proceedings. After ICE arrests an alien not subject to mandatory detention, an immigration officer makes an initial custody determination and may make further determinations during the course of formal removal proceedings, based on standards and criteria promulgated by the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ). 

 A lien s may be detained in an ICE facility or released on bond or conditional parole ; these individuals become part of the NDD . In any case, a lien s must attend all subsequent proceedings before an immigration judge (IJ) within DOJ ' s Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) . Detained aliens may request a review of the custody determination during a bond hearing before an IJ, unless they are subject to detention without bond by federal law.

 ICE's detention capacity limits the number of detainees that can be held at any given time. ICE currently oversees detainees in over 200 ICE-owned, private, state, and local facilities that house from fewer than 5 aliens to more than 2,000. ICE data indicate that 6 6,978 individuals were detained as of April 9, 2026. Between FY1996 and FY2025, the average annual total of detained individuals ranged from about 9,000 to 60,000. Currently, ICE possesses detention bedspace capacity for roughly 70,000 individuals and has considered plans to expand this capacity to over 90,000 in FY2026. 

 In contrast, the NDD refers to aliens who are subject to removal but are not detained . The docket includes individuals at any stage in the removal process . Individuals on the NDD remain under ICE supervision to help ensure that they regularly check in, comply with release conditions, attend court hearings, and comply with removal if so ordered. 

 The NDD Population

 Generally, the NDD population consists of aliens that 
 have been released at ICE's discretion following an initial or subsequent custody determination (as discussed previously); 

 are currently incarcerated in federal, state, and local facilities while serving sentences for criminal offenses; 

 have final removal orders but were granted temporary protection through withholding of removal or the Convention Against Torture (CAT) ;

 have final removal orders and are in the process of being repatriated; 

 have final removal orders but cannot be repatriated because their origin countries do not cooperate with the United States; 

 have final removal orders but absconded into the United States as fugitives ; and 

 unbeknownst to ICE, have voluntarily departed the United States or died and remain on the NDD erroneously. 
 ICE's most recently reported NDD population size of 7.3 million reflects its count of non-detained aliens as of February 26, 2026 ( Figure 1 ). All such individuals have been processed by ICE, including an estimated 1.6 million with final orders of removal . The NDD count relies on a cumulative list of removable aliens that is continuously updated; thus, it excludes those with a confirmed departure or death. Some aliens have been on the NDD for decades; others have been placed on it more recently. A fraction of NDD individuals are enrolled in ICE's Alternatives to Detention (ATD) program, which involves more intensive supervision than other NDD individuals who, in addition to attending all court hearings, typically must check in once a year with ICE. Currently, 180,000 individuals are on ATD.

 NDD Trends

 The NDD has more than tripled since FY2016 ( Figure 1 ). Recent NDD growth reflects high numbers of encounters (apprehensions) of aliens by the U.S. Border Patrol (USBP), part of DHS's Customs and Border Protection (CBP). From FY2016 through FY2020, annual USBP encounters at the Southwest border averaged about 470,000, and the NDD grew during that period from 2.2 million to 3.3 million unauthorized aliens. From FY2021 through FY2024, average annual encounters more than quadrupled to 1.9 million, boosting the NDD from 3.7 million to 7.7 million individuals. Since FY2025 (as of March 2026 ), USBP encounters have declined substantially. Increased ICE enforcement actions and removals that have prompted unauthorized aliens to self-deport have also reduced the NDD. Reportedly , about 72,000 aliens as of March 2026 have used a CBP incentive-based program to facilitate their voluntary departure and many others have left of their own accord.

 Figure 1. Estimated NDD Population, FY2016-FY2026*

 Notes: FY2026 * figure as of February 26, 2026.

 How the NDD Fluctuates

 The NDD increases with alien apprehensions and arrests and decreases when aliens are removed from the United States, or granted immigration relief (e.g., asylum) following immigration court proceedings. When border encounters are high, immigration officers may use their discretion to supervise individuals on the NDD instead of in limited detention space.  March 20, 2017 Washington , DC , United States Enforcement and Removal 
 DHS releases US Immigration and Customs Enforcement Declined Detainer Outcome Report

 WASHINGTON – The Department of Homeland Security today issued the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Declined Detainer Outcome Report required by President Donald J. Trump’s Executive Order , Enhancing Public Safety in the Interior of the United States , signed on January 25. This report will be issued weekly to highlight jurisdictions that choose not to cooperate with ICE detainers or requests for notification, therefore potentially endangering Americans. ICE places detainers on aliens who have been arrested on local criminal charges or who are in local custody and for whom ICE possesses probable cause to believe that they are removable from the United States, so that ICE can take custody of the alien when he or she is released from local custody.

 “When law enforcement agencies fail to honor immigration detainers and release serious criminal offenders, it undermines ICE’s ability to protect the public safety and carry out its mission,” said Acting ICE Director Thomas Homan. “Our goal is to build cooperative, respectful relationships with our law enforcement partners. We will continue collaborating with them to help ensure that illegal aliens who may pose a threat to our communities are not released onto the streets to potentially harm individuals living within our communities.” 

 The Declined Detainer Outcome Report is a weekly report that lists the jurisdictions that have declined to honor ICE detainers or requests for notification and includes examples of criminal charges associated with those released aliens. The report provides information on declined detainers and requests for notification for that reporting period. A jurisdiction’s appearance on this report is not an exclusive factor in determining a jurisdiction’s level of cooperation with ICE. This report is intended to provide the public with information regarding criminal actions committed by aliens and any jurisdiction that ignores or otherwise failed to honor any detainers or requests for notification with respect to such aliens.

Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers' - FactCheck.org 

 Skip to main content 

 FactCheck .org ® 

 A Project of The Annenberg Public Policy Center 

 This article is available in both English and Español 
 English 
 Español 

 In campaign appearances over the weekend in the swing state of Pennsylvania, former President Donald Trump and his running mate, Sen. JD Vance, falsely accused Vice President Kamala Harris of letting more than 13,000 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States.

 It’s true that there were 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder, as of July 21, who were not being detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. 

 But the “vast majority” of them entered the country prior to the Biden administration and had their custody status determined “long before this Administration,” the Department of Homeland Security said in a statement, noting that many were in prison. Also, the noncitizens include those who entered the country legally, such as green-card holders.

 Trump and Vance distorted the contents of a Sept. 25 letter that Patrick Lechleitner , the acting director of ICE, sent to Rep. Tony Gonzales . The Republican congressman had requested the number of noncitizens who had committed a crime but were not in ICE custody — a list known as the agency’s non-detained docket.

 Lechleitner’s response included a chart that showed there are 13,099 noncitizens convicted of murder who were not being detained by ICE. Homeland Security later clarified in its statement that “many” are in prisons, although it did not tell us how many are incarcerated when we inquired.

 Gonzales posted Lechleitner’s letter to X on Sept. 27. The next day, Vance referenced the 13,099 murderers at a campaign event in Newtown, Pennsylvania , and Trump did the same in Prairie du Chien, Wisconsin . A day later, Trump repeated the claim in Erie, Pennsylvania .

 Vance, Sept. 28: Do you know that there are 13,000 — I know some of you are nodding because some of you saw this — 13,000 illegal immigrant murderers in the United States of America right now. They’re in this country because Kamala Harris let them in this country. 

 Trump, Sept. 29: During her term, it’s not even believable, she let in 13,099 convicted murderers. Some of them had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven. One murdered six.

 In its statement, the Department of Homeland Security said data in Lechleitner’s letter had been “misinterpreted.”

 “The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this Administration,” the statement said. “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners.”

 Similarly, Michelle Mittelstadt , director of communications for the nonpartisan Migration Policy Institute, told us that people have been on the non-detained docket “for decades.”

 “There is a lot of confusion around the non-detained docket,” including “who is on it and how long they’ve been on it,” Mittelstadt said in an email. “This docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one. Significant numbers of people on the docket have been on it for decades.”

 For example, the ICE acting director said in his letter that there are 425,431 convicted criminals on the agency’s non-detained docket as of July 21. But, as Mittelstadt noted, ICE reported in a budget document “that there were 405,786 convicted criminal noncitizens on the non-detained docket in June 2021 – so the vast majority would have gotten on during the prior administrations as the Biden administration by then was just five months old.” The number of people on the docket has increased by nearly 5% in about three years.

 She also told us that “the non-detained docket includes not just unauthorized immigrants but green-card holders and noncitizens on long-term non-immigrant visas who have made themselves removable by virtue of a criminal conviction.”

 The ICE letter to Gonzales did show that, as of July 21, there were an additional 1,845 noncitizens on the non-detained docket who face murder charges. But, again, we don’t know when those 1,845 people entered the United States, how many of them may have entered illegally and when they committed their alleged crimes. We also do not know if they are being held by other local, state or federal law enforcement agencies. A Homeland Security spokesperson did not respond when we asked for such information.

 We asked the Trump campaign to respond to the evidence that contradicts its candidates’ claims that Harris let 13,099 “illegal immigrant murderers” into the United States. We also asked it to supply information about Trump’s claim that some of the 13,099 “had murdered 10 people, some murdered seven.” In response, Karoline Leavitt, Trump’s national press secretary, said Trump “will begin the largest mass deportation in history on day one.”

HTTP 200
Trump makes misleading claim about migrants with criminal records Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Migrants with criminal records - what new US data shows
 2 October 2024 Share Save Add as preferred on Google Jake Horton & Lucy Gilder BBC Verify Getty Images Newly-released figures about migrants with criminal convictions are being used to attack Democrats for the border policies under President Biden and Kamala Harris. 
 Donald Trump has used the figures to claim that "13,000 convicted murderers entered our country during her three and a half year period as Border Czar" and said they were allowed to "openly roam our country".
 But both claims are misleading.
 The new figures released by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) do show some 13,000 non-citizens convicted of homicide were on its records and not in its custody.
 However, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, said the figures cover a period of many years, and include migrants who entered the US under the Trump presidency and previous administrations.
 It also said that those on the list may not be in ICE custody but could be detained or in prison under the supervision of other agencies.
 What do the figures show? 
 The figures were released in a letter from ICE to Republican congressman Tony Gonzales, who had requested them. 
 They show that, as of July 2024, there were 425,431 non-citizens with criminal convictions on ICE’s "non-detained docket" - a database of people facing deportation proceedings but who are not held in ICE custody.
 Of these: 
 13,099 were convicted of homicide
 15,811 were convicted of sexual assault
 62,231 were convicted of assault
 However, a DHS statement said the data had been “misinterpreted". 
 “It also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners,” the DHS said.
 So, just because they are not being held by ICE, it does not mean they are all "roaming freely", as Trump claims. 
 “For example, Zacarias Moussaoui, who’s in a maximum security prison in Colorado for his role in the 9/11 attacks, is not currently detained by ICE so will likely be on that list,” says Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
 BBC Verify has asked the DHS how many are being held in detention by other agencies. 
 How many of them came under Biden and Harris?
 Trump said that the 13,000 convicted of killing someone entered the US under the Biden-Harris administration, but the ICE figures do not state when these people came to America.
 The DHS said: "The data goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more, the vast majority of whose custody determination was made long before this [Biden-Harris] administration."
 The non-detained docket is not routinely released and it is only published under certain circumstances on request - so we do not have exact numbers under each administration.
 The numbers were previously published in June 2021 , five months into the Biden presidency, which showed there were 405,431 convicted criminals on the list at that time.
 Before that, an official report published in August 2016 , towards the end of Barack Obama's presidency, showed 368,574.
 So, the list grew by almost 37,000 over five years, which includes Trump’s term in office.
 “This data shows a significant number would have gotten on the list during the prior administrations, and the docket has grown under multiple administrations, including the Trump one,” said Michelle Mittelstadt of the Migration Policy Institute.
 The overall number of non-citizens on the list has increased in recent years due to high levels of immigration under President Biden. 
 “Although, the number of people on the non-detained docket has increased substantially under the Biden administration, the number of people who are convicted criminals on the list hasn’t,” says Mr Reichlin-Melnick.
 In the letter, ICE does not specify how many of the non-citizens with criminal convictions on its list are illegal immigrants and how many entered the US with, for example, a green card.
 BBC Verify has asked for a breakdown.
 How many migrants have crossed the US border illegally?
 Why is it difficult to remove some criminals from the US?
 Part of the reason why overall numbers are high, experts say, is because of problems with deporting certain non-citizens who have committed crimes.
 “The US government cannot put a person on a commercial or government flight to return them to their country of nationality without agreement by that country,” says Michelle Mittelstadt.
 “Because the US has very limited diplomatic relations with Venezuela, Cuba, and Nicaragua, for example, deportation flights and returns to those countries are rare.”
 There are federal laws in place which mean people can only be held in detention for six months before the US government has to show they are a danger to the community.
 The UN Convention Against Torture means some immigrants, even those convicted of serious crimes, can have their deportation deferred if judges determine they would likely be tortured or persecuted in their home countries.
 DHS says it has removed over 180,000 non-citizens with criminal convictions since January 2021.

 Visa Sanctions Against Multiple Countries Pursuant to Section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act 

 Visa Sanctions Against Multiple Countries Pursuant to Section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act

 Recalcitrant Countries
 The U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) Enforcement and Removal Operations (ERO) mission is to protect the homeland through the arrest and removal of aliens who undermine the safety of our nation’s communities and the integrity of U.S. immigration laws.
 As a result, ICE removes aliens subject to final orders of removal to their country of citizenship.
 As part of the removal process, the U.S. government requests that foreign governments take appropriate steps to confirm the citizenship of individuals suspected to be their nationals — including conducting interviews when necessary; the timely issuance of travel documents, where appropriate; and the acceptance of the physical return of their nationals by scheduled commercial flights or, where necessary, special charter flights.
 Any lack of cooperation from the nation of origin delays, and in many cases, inhibits the removal process. Countries classified by ICE as uncooperative are also known as recalcitrant. Factors that could lead to a country being classified as recalcitrant include hindering ICE removal efforts by refusing to take the appropriate steps, as described above.
 Zadvydas v. Davis 
 Uncooperative countries significantly exacerbate the challenges presented to ICE by the U.S. Supreme Court’s decision in Zadvydas v. Davis , 533 U.S. 678 (2001). In this case, the Supreme Court ruled that:
 With narrow exceptions, aliens with final orders of removal — including aliens determined to pose threats to the community or considered flight risks — may not be detained by ICE beyond a presumptively reasonable period of six months if there is no “significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future”
 Delays in issuing travel documents or denying the acceptance of their nationals complicate ICE’s removal efforts as the agency has been legally required to release thousands of aliens, including those with serious criminal convictions
 Visa Sanctions
 When specific countries deny or delay accepting their nationals with final orders of removal from the United States, the U.S. government may issue visa sanctions as a means of encouraging the recalcitrant country to cooperate. In accordance with Section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), the Secretary of Homeland Security notifies the Secretary of State that multiple governments have denied or unreasonably delayed the acceptance of a national or nationals ordered removed from the United States.
 As a result, the Secretary of State may order U.S. consular officers at U.S. embassies and consulates in these countries to implement visa restrictions on certain categories of visa applicants. These sanctions may remain in place until the Secretary of Homeland Security notifies the Secretary of State that removal cooperation has improved to an acceptable level.

{"content": "# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE's most recent accounting to Congress found 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 15,811 with sexual assault convictions on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, and not one of them in ICE custody.
- The docket now holds 7.3 million people against roughly 70,000 detention beds, and state and local jails declined more than 25,000 ICE detainers between October 2022 and February 2025.
- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, put the 287(g) program in statute and require DHS to report publicly every criminal alien it releases.

### 1. A docket of convicted offenders

The most consequential number in the immigration debate did not come from an advocacy group. It came from ICE itself, in a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket carried 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges. Among the convicted: 13,099 homicide convictions, 15,811 sexual assault convictions and 62,231 assault convictions. Another 1,845 people on the same docket face murder charges.

Every one of them is outside ICE custody. Some are serving state or federal sentences and will walk out of a cell ICE does not control, at which point the agency has to find them again. Others were released outright after a custody determination. ICE has never published how many fall into each group, and it has not updated the accounting since.

The mismatch is arithmetic. The Congressional Research Service puts the non-detained docket at 7.3 million as of Feb. 26, 2026, including an estimated 1.6 million people with final orders of removal. ICE detention bedspace is roughly 70,000, and 66,978 people were in ICE custody on April 9, 2026. Beds for 70,000 cannot supervise a docket of 7.3 million, so the agency triages, and the convicted are triaged along with everyone else.

Two constraints in current law make that triage worse. Under the Supreme Court's decision in Zadvydas v. Davis, noncitizens with final removal orders, including those found to be threats to the community, generally may not be held past a presumptively reasonable six months if removal is not foreseeable. Because several countries delay or refuse to accept their own nationals, ICE states that it "has been legally required to release thousands of aliens, including those with serious criminal convictions." Detention capacity is not the only gap. Congress wrote the release valve into the statute, and Congress can close it.

### 2. What federal sentencing data show

The federal courts add a second, independent line of evidence. In fiscal 2024, 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 34.7 percent of all individuals sentenced that year. More than one in three. The Sentencing Commission reports that 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, which works out to nearly three in 10 of every individual sentenced federally.

Two offenses dominate that caseload. Immigration offenses accounted for 72.3 percent of noncitizen sentences and drug trafficking another 17.6 percent. Nor is the federal drug docket marginal to this debate: 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking sentences reported in fiscal 2024, roughly one in five, involved a noncitizen.

Critics of interior enforcement often reply that immigration prosecutions are paperwork cases. They are not. Unlawful entry and reentry prosecutions are how the system identifies, books and removes illegal aliens who are already in the country, and a reentry conviction almost always follows a prior removal. Every one of those 21,304 cases was a removable individual the federal government had in hand.

### 3. The state evidence: Texas

Only one state records immigration status in its criminal conviction data, and that is Texas. Analyses of Texas Department of Public Safety records by the Center for Immigration Studies, which count illegal immigrants identified during incarceration as well as at booking, find that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the state average. The dispute over how those records are classified is summarized in the data appendix to this brief.

State data matter because they show where the failure is not: Texas participates in 287(g), shares fingerprints through the federal system and honors detainers. Where enforcement tools are actually used, criminal aliens are identified before they are released, not after.

### 4. Detainers and sanctuary policies

The last link in the chain is the one that breaks most often: the ICE detainer, a request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours so ICE can take custody. ICE records obtained from the agency show that between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, more than 25,000 detainers were declined by state and local jails, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail released the alien without notifying ICE at all. More than half of the declined detainers, 52 percent, came from California facilities.

Laken Riley is the human cost of that practice. Jose Antonio Ibarra entered the United States illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022, and was released pending immigration proceedings. He was arrested by New York police on Aug. 31, 2023, on charges of acting in a manner to injure a child, and was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. On Feb. 22, 2024, he murdered Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, on a running trail at the University of Georgia. A Georgia judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act, signed Jan. 29, 2025, which requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assault of a law enforcement officer and other serious offenses, and lets states sue when the government fails to act. It was the right first step. Compliance, however, still depends on local cooperation, and where cooperation is refused, the federal government currently has no routine remedy.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate bed capacity dedicated to noncitizens with criminal convictions and pending violent charges, and amend 8 U.S.C. 1231(a)(6) to authorize detention beyond six months for criminal aliens whose countries refuse repatriation.

2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers and notification requests, enforce the information-sharing requirement at 8 U.S.C. 1373 and create a civil cause of action for victims of crimes committed by aliens released after a declined detainer.

3. **Put 287(g) in statute and fund it.** ICE has signed 2,679 agreements with state, local and tribal agencies in 38 states and two territories, including 1,924 task force agreements. Codify the program, including the task force model, so a future administration cannot rescind it, and fund officer training and reimbursement.

4. **Require DHS to report every criminal alien released.** Direct quarterly public reporting of noncitizens with criminal convictions on the non-detained docket by offense category, how many are incarcerated elsewhere, detainers declined by jurisdiction, and releases under the Zadvydas limit.

---

*The data appendix to this brief, published separately, provides tables, source lines and methodological notes for every figure cited above.*

# Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

## Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**By Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy**
Founders' Square Institute, Washington, D.C. | Oct. 27, 2026

### Executive summary

- ICE's most recent accounting to Congress found 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions and 15,811 with sexual assault convictions on its non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, and not one of them in ICE custody.
- The docket now holds 7.3 million people against roughly 70,000 detention beds, and state and local jails declined more than 25,000 ICE detainers between October 2022 and February 2025.
- Congress should fund detention for criminal aliens on the docket, penalize jurisdictions that refuse detainers, put the 287(g) program in statute and require DHS to report publicly every criminal alien it releases.

### 1. A docket of convicted offenders

The most consequential number in the immigration debate did not come from an advocacy group. It came from ICE itself, in a Sept. 25, 2024 letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales. As of July 21, 2024, the agency's non-detained docket carried 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions and another 222,141 with pending criminal charges. Among the convicted: 13,099 homicide convictions, 15,811 sexual assault convictions and 62,231 assault convictions. Another 1,845 people on the same docket face murder charges.

Every one of them is outside ICE custody. Some are serving state or federal sentences and will walk out of a cell ICE does not control, at which point the agency has to find them again. Others were released outright after a custody determination. ICE has never published how many fall into each group, and it has not updated the accounting since.

The mismatch is arithmetic. The Congressional Research Service puts the non-detained docket at 7.3 million as of Feb. 26, 2026, including an estimated 1.6 million people with final orders of removal. That docket stood at 2.2 million in fiscal 2016 and 7.7 million in fiscal 2024, so it has more than tripled in a decade. ICE detention bedspace is roughly 70,000, and 66,978 people were in ICE custody on April 9, 2026. Beds for 70,000 cannot supervise a docket of 7.3 million, so the agency triages, and convicted offenders are triaged along with everyone else. Only about 180,000 people on the docket are enrolled in alternatives to detention with intensive supervision. The rest check in periodically, if they check in at all.

Two constraints in current law make that triage worse. Under the Supreme Court's decision in Zadvydas v. Davis, noncitizens with final removal orders, including those found to be threats to the community, generally may not be held past a presumptively reasonable six months if removal is not foreseeable. Because several countries delay or refuse to accept their own nationals, ICE states that it "has been legally required to release thousands of aliens, including those with serious criminal convictions." Detention capacity is not the only gap. Congress wrote the release valve into the statute, and Congress can close it.

### 2. What federal sentencing data show

The federal courts add a second, independent line of evidence. In fiscal 2024, 21,304 noncitizens were sentenced in federal court, 34.7 percent of all individuals sentenced that year. More than one in three. The Sentencing Commission reports that 88.7 percent of those noncitizens were illegal aliens, which works out to nearly three in 10 of every individual sentenced federally.

Two offenses dominate that caseload. Immigration offenses accounted for 72.3 percent of noncitizen sentences and drug trafficking another 17.6 percent. Nor is the federal drug docket marginal to this debate: 3,603 of the 18,118 drug trafficking sentences reported in fiscal 2024, roughly one in five, involved a noncitizen.

Critics of interior enforcement answer that these are paperwork cases. They are not. Unlawful entry and reentry prosecutions are the mechanism by which the system identifies, books and removes illegal aliens already inside the country, and a reentry conviction necessarily follows a prior removal order. Every one of those 21,304 cases was a removable individual the federal government already had in hand. The question is whether he is held long enough to be removed.

### 3. The state evidence: Texas

Only one state records immigration status in its criminal conviction data, and that is Texas. Analyses of Texas Department of Public Safety records by the Center for Immigration Studies, which count illegal immigrants identified during incarceration as well as at booking, find that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the state average. The dispute over how those records are classified is summarized in the data appendix to this brief.

State data matter because they show where the failure is not: Texas participates in 287(g), shares fingerprints through the federal system and honors detainers. Where enforcement tools are actually used, criminal aliens are identified before they are released, not after.

### 4. Detainers and sanctuary policies

The last link in the chain is the one that breaks most often: the ICE detainer, a request that a jail hold a removable alien for up to 48 hours so ICE can take custody. ICE records obtained from the agency show that between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, more than 25,000 detainers were declined by state and local jails, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail released the alien without notifying ICE at all. More than half of the declined detainers, 52 percent, came from California facilities. Those records were the subject of congressional testimony in March 2026, and they remain the best available measure of a policy choice made deliberately by hundreds of jails and prisons.

Laken Riley is the human cost of that practice. Jose Antonio Ibarra entered the United States illegally near El Paso on Sept. 8, 2022, and was released pending immigration proceedings. He was arrested by New York police on Aug. 31, 2023, on charges of acting in a manner to injure a child, and was released before ICE could lodge a detainer. On Feb. 22, 2024, he murdered Riley, a 22-year-old nursing student, on a running trail at the University of Georgia. A Georgia judge convicted him in November 2024 and sentenced him to life in prison without parole.

Congress responded with the Laken Riley Act, signed Jan. 29, 2025, which requires detention of illegal aliens charged with theft, burglary, assault of a law enforcement officer and other serious offenses, and lets states sue when the government fails to act. It was the right first step. Compliance, however, still depends on local cooperation, and where cooperation is refused, the federal government currently has no routine remedy.

### 5. Recommendations

1. **Fund detention for criminal aliens on the non-detained docket.** Appropriate bed capacity dedicated to noncitizens with criminal convictions and pending violent charges, and amend 8 U.S.C. 1231(a)(6) to authorize detention beyond six months for criminal aliens whose countries refuse repatriation.

2. **Mandate detainer compliance and penalize sanctuary jurisdictions.** Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers and notification requests, enforce the information-sharing requirement at 8 U.S.C. 1373 and create a civil cause of action for victims of crimes committed by aliens released after a declined detainer.

3. **Put 287(g) in statute and fund it.** ICE has signed 2,679 agreements with state, local and tribal agencies in 38 states and two territories, including 1,924 task force agreements. Codify the program, including the task force model, so a future administration cannot rescind it, and fund officer training and reimbursement.

4. **Require DHS to report every criminal alien released.** Direct quarterly public reporting of noncitizens with criminal convictions on the non-detained docket by offense category, how many are incarcerated elsewhere, detainers declined by jurisdiction, and releases under the Zadvydas limit.

---

*The data appendix to this brief, published separately, provides tables, source lines and methodological notes for every figure cited above.*

 U.S. immigration enforcement personnel carry out an arrest. Credit: Wikimedia Commons / usicegov 

 Texas accounted for a quarter of all U.S. immigration arrests in July as the Trump White House stepped up its use of local and state law enforcement to carry out its mass-deportation agenda, the Marshall Project reports .

 Some 2,000 state and local law enforcement agencies have signed agreements with the feds to conduct immigration stops and turn over migrants who end up in local jails, according to an analysis by the criminal justice-focused nonprofit newsroom.

 Sign up 

 The White House shifted to the cooperative approach after high-profile surges in Democrat-led cities yielded severe public backlash and led to the fatal shootings of Minneapolis residents Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal agents.

 Cooperation has been especially strong in Republican-led states, the Marshall Project reports, and Texas, led by Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, has been among the most willing partners in this quieter crackdown. Abbott, a Trump loyalist, has increasingly made anti-immigrant sentiment part of his political brand .

 “We call it the ‘shadow surge,’” Jill Garvey, director of States at the Core, a group that supports grassroots resistance to authoritarian threats, told the Marshall Project. “It’s this much quieter, but no less violent or deadly, enforcement.”

 Since June, ICE has set new monthly records for signing up local law enforcement partners, the Marshall Project reports, citing agency documents. As a result, immigration arrests from March through July increased from the same period last year in all but four states, according to data published by the Deportation Data Project at UC Berkeley and UCLA.

 Texas immigration arrests accounted for 10,329 of July’s total of 41,748 busts nationwide, the universities’ database shows . Florida, the state with the next-highest number of arrests, recorded just half of Texas’ total at 5,468.

 Growing Texas cooperation 

 The increased use of state and local police agencies has made it harder for observers to distinguish routine traffic stops from targeted immigration actions, Garvey told the Marshall Project. That, in turn, has made it harder for ordinary citizens to hold the administration accountable as it steps up immigration sweeps. 

 The Texas Department of Public Safety is far from the only Lone Star State law enforcement agency partnering with ICE in its new under-the-radar approach. As of this month, 432 law enforcement agencies in the state have signed a total of 514 agreements with ICE for any of its three types of cooperation partnerships, the Texas Tribune reports .

 More than half of those agreements — a total of 314 — are for ICE’s most-controversial partnership, the “task force model” established by Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which gives local cops the authority to question people about their immigration status during traffic stops and other routine police work.

 Last month, Democratic federal and state lawmakers called on six small San Antonio-area communities to end their task force agreements with ICE. The elected officials maintain the deals make residents less safe, expose people to racial profiling and undermine trust in law enforcement.

 “ICE has become an abusive and rogue organization at this point,” San Antonio U.S. Rep. Joaquin Castro, an outspoken critic of Trump’s mass deportation program, said during a press conference calling out the municipalities. “And for that reason, all of these relationships need to be reexamined.”

{"content": "# Data Appendix - Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14

**Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show**
Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

One table is provided for each figure used in the brief. Source lines follow the FSI style sheet: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL. Population, timeframe and methodology notes are carried here rather than in the brief, the fact sheet or the stat cards.

---

## Table 1. Noncitizens with criminal convictions on ICE's non-detained docket

*As of July 21, 2024. Figures are individuals.*

| Category | Individuals |
|---|---|
| Noncitizens with criminal convictions on the non-detained docket | 425,431 |
| Homicide convictions | 13,099 |
| Sexual assault convictions | 15,811 |
| Assault convictions | 62,231 |
| Noncitizens with pending criminal charges | 222,141 |
| Facing murder charges (subset of pending charges) | 1,845 |

**Source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Patrick J. Lechleitner), Letter to Rep. Tony Gonzales, Sept. 25, 2024, https://homeland.house.gov/wp-content/uploads/2024/09/24-01143-ICEs-Signed-Response-to-Representative-Tony-Gonzales.pdf

**Notes**
- ICE's "non-detained docket" is the agency's list of noncitizens in the removal process who are not in ICE custody. It is not a list of people at large: DHS states the data "goes back decades; it includes individuals who entered the country over the past 40 years or more" and that it "also includes many who are under the jurisdiction or currently incarcerated by federal, state or local law enforcement partners." (Department of Homeland Security statement, September 2024, quoted in FactCheck.org, "Trump, Vance Wrong About 'Illegal Immigrant Murderers,'" Sept. 30, 2024, https://www.factcheck.org/2024/09/trump-vance-wrong-about-illegal-immigrant-murderers/)
- ICE did not report how many of the individuals listed are incarcerated by another authority, and did not break the docket down by immigration status. The totals include lawful permanent residents and other noncitizens made removable by a conviction.
- Comparable earlier counts of convicted criminals on the non-detained docket were 368,574 (August 2016) and 405,431 (June 2021), indicating a cumulative, multi-administration backlog rather than a single-year cohort. (BBC Verify, "Migrants with criminal records: what new US data show," Oct. 2, 2024, https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cz04y0371lvo)
- The July 21, 2024 accounting is the most recent ICE has published. DHS has not released an update; that reporting gap is the subject of Recommendation 4 in the brief.

---

## Table 2. ICE non-detained docket size and detention capacity

| Measure | Value | As of |
|---|---|---|
| Non-detained docket population | 7.3 million | Feb. 26, 2026 |
| Of which, with final orders of removal | ~1.6 million | Feb. 2026 |
| Non-detained docket population, FY2016 | 2.2 million | FY2016 |
| Non-detained docket population, FY2024 | 7.7 million | FY2024 |
| Individuals in ICE custody | 66,978 | Apr. 9, 2026 |
| ICE detention bedspace capacity | ~70,000 | 2026 |
| Enrolled in Alternatives to Detention | 180,000 | 2026 |

**Source:** Congressional Research Service, *Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and the Non-Detained Docket (NDD)*, IF13208, Apr. 24, 2026, https://crsreports.congress.gov/product/pdf/IF/IF13208 (mirror: https://www.everycrsreport.com/reports/IF13208.html)

**Notes**
- CRS figures are drawn from ICE, including the ICE Office of Legislative Affairs for FY2025-FY2026. The FY2026 figure is a point-in-time count as of Feb. 26, 2026.
- The non-detained docket includes people who are currently incarcerated in federal, state and local facilities; people with final orders who cannot be repatriated because their countries will not accept them; fugitives with final orders; and, per CRS, some individuals who have departed or died and remain on the docket erroneously. The count is a cumulative list of removable aliens, continuously updated.
- Because of those composition effects, the docket total should not be read as a count of convicted offenders or of people at large. Table 1 reports the criminal-conviction subset separately.

---

## Table 3. Federal sentencing of noncitizens, FY2024

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| All individuals sentenced in federal court | 61,342 |
| Non-U.S. citizens sentenced | 21,304 (34.7%) |
| Illegal aliens, share of sentenced noncitizens | 88.7% |
| Legal aliens, share of sentenced noncitizens | 8.5% |
| Illegal aliens, share of all individuals sentenced (FSI calculation) | 30.8% |
| Noncitizen sentences under the immigration guideline | 72.3% |
| Noncitizen sentences under the drug trafficking guideline | 17.6% |
| Drug trafficking sentences involving a noncitizen | 3,603 of 18,118 (19.9%) |

**Sources:** U.S. Sentencing Commission, *Quick Facts on Federally Sentenced Non-U.S. Citizens*, FY2024, 2025, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/quick-facts/Non-Citizen_FY24.pdf; U.S. Sentencing Commission, *2024 Sourcebook of Federal Sentencing Statistics*, Table 9, 2025, https://www.ussc.gov/sites/default/files/pdf/research-and-publications/annual-reports-and-sourcebooks/2024/Table09.pdf

**Notes**
- Percentages for offense type are the most common guidelines under which noncitizens were sentenced; the drug trafficking count of 3,603 is by offense type of conviction. The two classifications differ slightly.
- The 30.8 percent figure is an FSI calculation (34.7% of all individuals sentenced multiplied by 88.7% illegal aliens among noncitizens).
- Context on trend: GAO reports the number of noncitizens sentenced for federal crimes fell 27 percent from FY2018 (about 29,500) to FY2023 (about 21,500), with immigration offenses the most common offense type (about 76 percent) throughout. (U.S. Government Accountability Office, *Noncitizens in the U.S.: Public Information on Federal Incarcerations*, GAO-24-107598, Sept. 3, 2024, https://www.gao.gov/products/gao-24-107598)
- The Commission has since published FY2025 data showing 28,886 noncitizens sentenced, 44 percent of all individuals sentenced. See editor's note in the production memo; the brief uses the FY2024 figures in the author's source tables.

---

## Table 4. Declined ICE detainers in non-cooperating jurisdictions

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Detainers declined by state and local jails | 25,000+ |
| Releases without adequate notification to ICE | 1,400+ |
| Share of declined detainers from California facilities | 52% |

**Source:** Jessica M. Vaughan, Center for Immigration Studies, *Statement before the U.S. Senate Committee on the Judiciary, Subcommittee on the Constitution, "Sanctuary Jurisdiction Policies and Federalism,"* Mar. 25, 2026, https://www.judiciary.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/150abe42-c7cd-d0d2-6ea3-cd1bfc1e0813/2026-03-25-PM_Testimony_Vaughan.pdf

**Notes**
- Figures are from ICE records obtained by the Center for Immigration Studies under the Freedom of Information Act; the period covered is Oct. 1, 2022, through Feb. 6, 2025. The same figures were submitted to the U.S. House Committee on the Judiciary on Mar. 4, 2026.
- ICE cautions that a jurisdiction's appearance on declined-detainer reporting "is not an exclusive factor in determining a jurisdiction's level of cooperation." (U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, *DHS Releases ICE Declined Detainer Outcome Report*, Mar. 20, 2017, https://www.ice.gov/news/releases/dhs-releases-us-immigration-and-customs-enforcement-declined-detainer-outcome-report)
- A detainer is a request that a jail hold a removable alien up to 48 hours beyond the scheduled release so ICE can assume custody. A declined detainer is a release that occurs without a transfer.

---

## Table 5. ICE 287(g) agreements with state, local and tribal agencies

*As of Oct. 15, 2026.*

| Model | Agencies | States and territories |
|---|---|---|
| Jail Enforcement Model | 183 | 29 states, 1 territory |
| Warrant Service Officer Model | 572 | 34 states |
| Task Force Model | 1,924 | 32 states, 2 territories |
| **Total memorandums of agreement** | **2,679** | **38 states, 2 territories** |

**Source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, *Delegation of Immigration Authority Section 287(g) Immigration and Nationality Act*, updated Oct. 14, 2026, https://www.ice.gov/identify-and-arrest/287g

**Notes**
- Counts are agreements, not agencies; a law enforcement agency may hold more than one model agreement, so agency totals by model do not sum to the agreement total.
- The expansion follows Executive Order 14159 (Jan. 20, 2025), which directs ICE to authorize 287(g) agreements "to the maximum extent permitted by law."

---

## Table 6. Texas DPS conviction data, homicide, 2013-2022

*Counter-research carried in the appendix only, per FSI style sheet B3.*

- The Cato Institute (Alex Nowrasteh), using Texas Department of Public Safety data for 2013-2022, reports a homicide conviction rate of 2.2 per 100,000 for illegal immigrants against 3.0 per 100,000 for native-born Americans, and finds illegal immigrants 26 percent less likely to be convicted of homicide. **Source:** Cato Institute, *Illegal Immigrant Murderers in Texas, 2013-2022*, June 2024, https://www.cato.org/policy-analysis/illegal-immigrant-murderers-texas-2013-2022
- The Center for Immigration Studies disputes those denominators, arguing the analysis misses illegal immigrants identified only after incarceration and misclassifies them as native-born, and concludes that illegal immigrants in Texas are convicted of homicide and sexual assault at higher rates than the state average. **Source:** Center for Immigration Studies (Kennedy, Richwine and Camarota), *Misuse of Texas Data Understates Illegal Immigrant Criminality*, Oct. 11, 2022, https://cis.org/Report/Misuse-Texas-Data-Understates-Illegal-Immigrant-Criminality

**Notes**
- Texas is the only state that records immigration status in its criminal conviction records, which is why both analyses use it.
- Cato notes data quality caveats for non-homicide offenses, and CIS notes significant uncertainties remain, especially for lesser offenses. Neither estimate is a federal primary source, and the two disagree on classification of offenders whose status is determined after conviction.

---

## Table 7. Case record: Jose Antonio Ibarra and the murder of Laken Riley

| Event | Date | Detail |
|---|---|---|
| Unlawful entry near El Paso, Texas | Sept. 8, 2022 | Apprehended by CBP, released pending immigration proceedings |
| Arrest by New York police | Aug. 31, 2023 | Charged with acting in a manner to injure a child and a motor vehicle violation; released before ICE could lodge a detainer |
| Murder of Laken Riley, 22, Athens, Georgia | Feb. 22, 2024 | Nursing student attacked on a running trail at the University of Georgia |
| Conviction and sentence | Nov. 20, 2024 | Athens-Clarke County Superior Court, Judge H. Patrick Haggard; life in prison without parole |
| Laken Riley Act, Public Law 119-1 | Jan. 29, 2025 | Requires detention of certain aliens charged with theft, burglary, assault of a law enforcement officer and other offenses; authorizes state suits against the federal government |

**Sources:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement statement of Feb. 25, 2024, as reported in CBS News, "Suspect in murder of Georgia nursing student entered U.S. illegally, ICE says," February 2024, https://www.cbsnews.com/news/jose-ibarra-suspect-murder-georgia-nursing-student-illegal-entry-venezuela/; Associated Press, "Man convicted of killing Laken Riley sentenced to life in prison without parole," Nov. 20, 2024, https://apnews.com/article/georgia-nursing-student-laken-riley-immigrant-d8d75ccc6d81e7ea78eb7890829d9fc9c; S.5, Public Law 119-1, https://www.congress.gov/bill/119th-congress/senate-bill/5

---

## Table 8. Statutory and judicial limits on detention of criminal aliens

| Provision | Effect |
|---|---|
| *Zadvydas v. Davis*, 533 U.S. 678 (2001) | With narrow exceptions, noncitizens with final removal orders, including those found to threaten the community, may not be held beyond a presumptively reasonable six months absent a significant likelihood of removal in the reasonably foreseeable future |
| ICE reporting on the decision | ICE states that because of uncooperative countries and travel document delays it "has been legally required to release thousands of aliens, including those with serious criminal convictions" |
| INA Section 243(d), 8 U.S.C. 1253(d) | Authorizes visa sanctions against countries that deny or unreasonably delay acceptance of their nationals ordered removed |

**Source:** U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, *Visa Sanctions Against Multiple Countries Pursuant to Section 243(d) of the Immigration and Nationality Act*, updated Jan. 22, 2025, https://www.ice.gov/remove/visa-sanctions

---

*Prepared for the Director of Publications. Draft, not for publication or distribution.*

{"content": "# Criminal Aliens and Public Safety: What the Federal Data Show

**Border Security & Public Safety Brief No. 14 | Fact Sheet for Hill Offices**
Brett Kessler, Senior Fellow for Immigration Policy | Founders' Square Institute | Oct. 27, 2026

## Key statistics

**1. 13,099 noncitizens with homicide convictions were on ICE's non-detained docket as of July 21, 2024, and none was in ICE custody.** The same docket carried 15,811 sexual assault convictions and 62,231 assault convictions.[1]

**2. 425,431 noncitizens with criminal convictions were on that docket, plus another 222,141 with pending criminal charges**, including 1,845 facing murder charges.[1]

**3. The non-detained docket holds 7.3 million people against roughly 70,000 ICE detention beds.** An estimated 1.6 million people on the docket already have final orders of removal; ICE held 66,978 people on April 9, 2026.[2]

**4. The docket has more than tripled in a decade**, from 2.2 million in fiscal 2016 to 7.7 million in fiscal 2024, and it stood at 7.3 million on Feb. 26, 2026.[2]

**5. Noncitizens accounted for 34.7 percent of everyone sentenced in federal court in fiscal 2024: 21,304 of 61,342 individuals.** Nearly nine in 10 of them, 88.7 percent, were illegal aliens, which is nearly three in 10 of the entire federal sentencing population.[3]

**6. Immigration offenses drove 72.3 percent of noncitizen federal sentences in fiscal 2024, and drug trafficking another 17.6 percent.** One in five federal drug trafficking sentences, 3,603 of 18,118, involved a noncitizen.[3]

**7. More than 25,000 ICE detainers were declined by state and local jails between Oct. 1, 2022, and Feb. 6, 2025, and in more than 1,400 cases the jail released the alien without notifying ICE.** Fifty-two percent of declined detainers came from California facilities.[4]

**8. ICE has signed 2,679 287(g) agreements with state, local and tribal agencies in 38 states and two territories as of Oct. 15, 2026, including 1,924 task force agreements.**[5]

## What Congress should do

- Appropriate detention capacity dedicated to noncitizens with criminal convictions and amend 8 U.S.C. 1231(a)(6) to allow detention beyond six months for criminal aliens whose countries refuse repatriation.[6]
- Condition federal law enforcement funding on honoring ICE detainers and enforce 8 U.S.C. 1373.[6]
- Codify 287(g), including the task force model, and fund officer training and reimbursement.[5]
- Require DHS to report quarterly every criminal alien released, every declined detainer by jurisdiction and every release under the *Zadvydas* limit.[6]
